values.value: • Drive a dated close plan immediately while momentum is high. • List all remaining approvals, documents, and buyer actions that must happen before closure. • Confirm commercial, legal, procurement, and implementation readiness now. • Use tight follow-ups with owners and dates. • Protect against last-minute slippage by surfacing blockers early.
15|<30 days
Buyer may say, 'We are trying to close quickly.' Response: 'Great. Then let us map the remaining approvals and documents now so nothing slows the close unexpectedly.'
Good. Build a close plan now with exact dates, approvers, and response commitments.
Low risk. Use the near-term window well.
Ask: 'To hit that timeline, what needs to happen this week from both our sides?'
<30 days

• Use the medium horizon to close gaps before the deal reaches final pressure. • Break the next 30 to 60 days into discovery close, proposal, validation, approval, and closure stages. • Ask which internal events or meetings will determine movement. • Create intermediate commitments so the deal keeps moving. • Do not wait passively for the expected close window.
Buyer may say, 'This will likely take a bit of time.' Response: 'That is fine. Let us break that window into the specific steps that will move it forward.'
Bring structure to the middle window. Map milestones so it does not quietly become 90+ days.
Risk: Moderate delay risk if milestones are loose.
Ask: 'What approvals or discussions sit between now and the decision date?'
30-60 days

• A longer cycle needs stronger control, not just patience. • Find what must happen to bring the timeline forward or at least keep it real. • Build urgency through impact, budget timing, admissions, planning cycles, or business deadlines. • Keep multi-stakeholder engagement active so the deal does not cool off. • Convert a vague long cycle into a managed plan.
Buyer may say, 'This is a longer-cycle decision.' Response: 'Understood. I would like to know what has to happen across that period so we can keep the deal active and relevant.'
Find out why this is so far out. Either there is low urgency, internal dependency, or weak sponsorship.
Risk: Long-dated deals lose energy.
Ask: 'What would need to change for this to move faster than the current window?'
60-90 days

• This is a forecasting weakness and usually means the buyer process is still unclear. • Ask what event, approval, meeting, or milestone would signal real closure timing. • Map the buying path backwards from their likely decision point. • Use that to define a realistic date range instead of guesswork. • Do not commit internally to a close month without buyer evidence.
15|Not sure
Buyer may say, 'Too early to say.' Response: 'That is okay. Even a likely decision event or milestone would help us pace this correctly.'
Do not accept a floating timeline. Ask for the trigger event, budget cycle, or internal milestone that sets the date.
High risk: No close date discipline.
Ask: 'What event or approval will decide when this actually moves?'
Not sure
